title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MaxDiff, also called Best-Worst Scaling, is a survey method for measuring preference. Instead of asking people to rate every item on a 1 to 10 scale, MaxDiff asks people to make trade-offs. On each screen, a respondent sees a small set of items and chooses the one they like most and the one they like least.
This is useful because people are usually better at choosing between options than at using a numeric rating scale consistently. One person may give many 9s and 10s, while another person may be stricter and give mostly 6s and 7s. MaxDiff reduces that problem because it forces real differentiation.
In this assignment, the items are the core MSBA classes. I estimate class preferences in three ways:

A simple counts analysis: percent picked best minus percent picked worst.
A multinomial logit model estimated by maximum likelihood.
The same multinomial logit model estimated with a Bayesian Metropolis-Hastings sampler.

My expectation is that the three methods should mostly agree on the strongest and weakest classes. The middle of the ranking may move around more because the differences between those classes are smaller.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Counts Analysis
The simplest analysis is the counts score. For each class, I calculate how often it was selected as best and how often it was selected as worst, relative to the number of times it was shown. The score is:
\[
\text{score}_j = \%\text{best}_j - \%\text{worst}_j
\]
A positive score means the class was more often chosen as best than worst. A negative score means the class was more often chosen as worst than best.


Code
counts = (
    choices.groupby("item")
    .agg(
        times_shown=("response", "size"),
        times_best=("response", lambda x: int((x == 1).sum())),
        times_worst=("response", lambda x: int((x == -1).sum()))
    )
    .reset_index()
    .merge(labels, on="item")
)

counts["pct_best"] = counts["times_best"] / counts["times_shown"]
counts["pct_worst"] = counts["times_worst"] / counts["times_shown"]
counts["counts_score"] = counts["pct_best"] - counts["pct_worst"]
counts["counts_rank"] = counts["counts_score"].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)
counts_table = counts.sort_values("counts_score", ascending=False)[[
    "item", "label", "times_shown", "times_best", "times_worst", "pct_best", "pct_worst", "counts_score", "counts_rank"

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
section: From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
text:
From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
For the MNL model, each class gets a utility coefficient, \(\beta_j\). A higher coefficient means the class is more preferred.
For a task showing four classes, the probability that class \(j\) is chosen as best is:
\[
P(\text{best}=j) = \frac{\exp(\beta_j)}{\sum_{k \in \text{shown}} \exp(\beta_k)}
\]
After the best item is chosen, the worst item is modeled from the remaining three classes using flipped utility. A high-utility item should be unlikely to be chosen as worst, so the worst-choice probability uses \(-\beta_j\):
\[
P(\text{worst}=j \mid \text{best chosen}) = \frac{\exp(-\beta_j)}{\sum_{k \in \text{shown except best}} \exp(-\beta_k)}
\]
One technical issue is identification. Adding the same constant to every \(\beta\) does not change the choice probabilities. To solve this, I set item 1 as the reference class with \(\beta_1 = 0\) and estimate the other nine coefficients.


Code
K = J - 1  # estimate beta_2 through beta_10; beta_1 is fixed at 0

def full_beta(beta_free):
    """Insert reference beta_1 = 0."""
    return np.r_[0.0, np.asarray(beta_free)]

def log_likelihood(beta_free):
    """Vectorized MaxDiff log-likelihood."""
    beta = full_beta(beta_free)
    v = beta[shown_mat]  # n_tasks x 4

    best_part = beta[best_idx] - logsumexp(v, axis=1)

    # For the worst choice, remove the item already picked as best.
    remaining_mask = shown_mat != best_idx[:, None]
    neg_v_remaining = np.where(remaining_mask, -v, -np.inf)
    worst_part = -beta[worst_idx] - logsumexp(neg_v_remaining, axis=1)

    return float(np.sum(best_part + worst_part))

def neg_log_likelihood(beta_free):
    return -log_likelihood(beta_free)

def log_likelihood_grad(beta_free):
    """Gradient of the log-likelihood for beta_2 through beta_10."""
    beta = full_beta(beta_free)
    v = beta[shown_mat]

    # Best choice contribution: chosen best minus softmax over shown items.
    p_best = np.exp(v - logsumexp(v, axis=1, keepdims=True))
    grad = np.zeros(J)
    np.add.at(grad, best_idx, 1.0)
    for col in range(shown_mat.shape[1]):
        np.add.at(grad, shown_mat[:, col], -p_best[:, col])

    # Worst choice contribution: chosen worst gets -1; remaining items get softmax over -utility.
    remaining_mask = shown_mat != best_idx[:, None]
    neg_v_remaining = np.where(remaining_mask, -v, -np.inf)
    p_worst = np.exp(neg_v_remaining - logsumexp(neg_v_remaining, axis=1, keepdims=True))
    np.add.at(grad, worst_idx, -1.0)
    for col in range(shown_mat.shape[1]):
        np.add.at(grad, shown_mat[:, col], p_worst[:, col])

    return grad[1:]

def neg_log_likelihood_grad(beta_free):
    return -log_likelihood_grad(beta_free)

# Small check: the likelihood at zero is finite.
log_likelihood(np.zeros(K))


-1689.7365218558405

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MNL via Maximum Likelihood
The log-likelihood sums the probability of the observed best and worst choices across all tasks:
\[
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{\text{tasks}} \left[\beta_{j_b^*} - \log \sum_{j \in \text{shown}} \exp(\beta_j) - \beta_{j_w^*} - \log \sum_{j \in \text{shown} \setminus j_b^*} \exp(-\beta_j) \right]
\]
I maximize this log-likelihood using numerical optimization.


Code
mle = minimize(
    neg_log_likelihood,
    x0=np.zeros(K),
    jac=neg_log_likelihood_grad,
    method="BFGS",
    options={"gtol": 1e-6, "maxiter": 1000}
)

mle_success = mle.success
mle_message = mle.message
beta_mle_free = mle.x
beta_mle = full_beta(beta_mle_free)

# Approximate covariance matrix from the inverse Hessian returned by BFGS.
# Item 1 is fixed, so its SE is 0 by construction.
cov_free = np.asarray(mle.hess_inv)
se_free = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov_free))
se_mle = np.r_[0.0, se_free]

shares_mle = np.exp(beta_mle) / np.exp(beta_mle).sum()

mle_table = labels.copy()
mle_table["beta_mle"] = beta_mle
mle_table["se_mle"] = se_mle
mle_table["mle_share"] = shares_mle
mle_table["mle_rank"] = mle_table["mle_share"].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)

print("Optimization success:", mle_success)
print("Optimizer message:", mle_message)
print("Final log-likelihood:", round(log_likelihood(beta_mle_free), 2))

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MNL via Bayesian Estimation
The Bayesian model uses the same MNL likelihood, but adds a prior distribution on the coefficients. I use a weakly informative normal prior:
\[
\boldsymbol{\beta} \sim N(0, 10I)
\]
This prior is wide enough to let the data drive the result, but it also prevents absurdly large estimates. I estimate the posterior distribution using a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler.


Code
prior_sd = np.sqrt(10)

def log_prior(beta_free):
    return np.sum(-0.5 * (beta_free / prior_sd) ** 2 - np.log(prior_sd * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)))

def log_posterior(beta_free):
    return log_likelihood(beta_free) + log_prior(beta_free)

def mh_sampler(beta0, n_iter=15000, step=0.18):
    beta = np.asarray(beta0).copy()
    draws = np.zeros((n_iter, len(beta)))
    lp = log_posterior(beta)
    accept = 0
    for t in range(n_iter):
        beta_star = beta + np.random.normal(0, step, size=len(beta))
        lp_star = log_posterior(beta_star)
        if np.log(np.random.rand()) < lp_star - lp:
            beta = beta_star
            lp = lp_star
            accept += 1
        draws[t, :] = beta
    return draws, accept / n_iter




Code
# Starting at the MLE helps the chain settle quickly.
draws_free, accept_rate = mh_sampler(beta_mle_free, n_iter=8000, step=0.18)
burn = int(0.25 * len(draws_free))
post_free = draws_free[burn:, :]
post_full = np.column_stack([np.zeros(len(post_free)), post_free])

accept_rate

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Discussion
The substantive result is that students do not view all MSBA classes equally. Some courses are clearly more preferred, while others are more often selected as least preferred. This is useful information for understanding student interest, but it should not be interpreted as a perfect measure of course quality. Students may choose based on instructor reputation, topic familiarity, career goals, or how difficult they expect a class to be.
The three methods answer the same general question in different ways. Counts analysis is the best quick summary. It is easy to explain on a dashboard because it only uses best and worst percentages. MLE MNL is stronger when we want a formal model and standard errors. Bayesian MNL is useful when we care about uncertainty in derived quantities, such as preference shares, or when we want to extend the model later to estimate individual-level preferences.
There are also caveats. The survey respondents are a self-selected sample of MSBA students, so the results may not generalize to all future students. The timing of the survey matters too. Students who have already taken a class may judge it differently from students who only know the course title. Presentation order and recent conversations with classmates could also influence choices.
If I had more time, I would explore individual-level heterogeneity. For example, students interested in marketing analytics may rank the classes differently from students focused on engineering, product analytics, or consulting. A hierarchical Bayesian model would be a natural next step because it could estimate both the overall ranking and each student’s personal preference pattern.

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
In April 1992, New Jersey increased its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour. Card and Krueger (1994) examined whether this policy reduced employment in the fast-food industry. Their study became one of the most influential empirical papers in labor economics because it challenged the traditional prediction that higher minimum wages necessarily reduce employment.
The authors compared fast-food restaurants in New Jersey to similar restaurants in eastern Pennsylvania, where the minimum wage did not change. This creates a natural difference-in-differences (DID) research design, where Pennsylvania serves as the control group and New Jersey serves as the treated group.
The goal of this replication is to reproduce the paper’s main employment result using the publicly available dataset.

Conclusion
This replication broadly confirms the main findings of Card and Krueger (1994). Using the publicly available dataset, I find no evidence that the 1992 New Jersey minimum wage increase reduced fast-food employment. title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
On my website’s homepage, I invite visitors to sign up for a newsletter. However, I am unsure which wording is more effective at encouraging users to subscribe.
To answer this question, I compare two different calls to action (CTAs):

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

To determine which version performs better, I run an A/B test. In an A/B test, visitors are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Each group sees a different version of the CTA, and we compare their sign-up rates.
By analyzing the difference in performance between the two groups, we can make data-driven decisions about which CTA is more effective.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
On my website’s homepage, I invite visitors to sign up for a newsletter. However, I am unsure which wording is more effective at encouraging users to subscribe.
To answer this question, I compare two different calls to action (CTAs):

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

To determine which version performs better, I run an A/B test. In an A/B test, visitors are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Each group sees a different version of the CTA, and we compare their sign-up rates.
By analyzing the difference in performance between the two groups, we can make data-driven decisions about which CTA is more effective.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
Each visitor either signs up or does not sign up, so their outcome can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable. Let \(\pi\) denote the probability of signing up.
Because the CTA may influence behavior, we allow different probabilities for each group:

\(\pi_A\): probability of signing up under CTA A
\(\pi_B\): probability of signing up under CTA B

The key quantity of interest is the difference in conversion rates:
\[
\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B
\]
We estimate this using the difference in sample means:
\[
\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B
\]
Since each observation is either 0 or 1, the sample mean is simply the proportion of users who signed up. Therefore:

\(\bar{X}_A = \hat{\pi}_A\)
\(\bar{X}_B = \hat{\pi}_B\)

So \(\hat\theta\) represents the observed difference in sign-up rates between the two CTAs.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data
In real-world settings, we do not know the true probabilities \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\). However, for this exercise, we set them manually to study how our estimator behaves when the truth is known.
Suppose:

\(\pi_A = 0.22\)
\(\pi_B = 0.18\)

So the true difference is \(\theta = 0.04\).
We simulate 1,000 visitors for each group.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
from scipy.stats import norm

np.random.seed(42)

n = 1000
pi_A = 0.22
pi_B = 0.18

A = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, n)
B = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, n)

theta_hat = A.mean() - B.mean()
theta_hat

np.float64(0.038000000000000006)


The estimated difference in conversion rates from this simulated experiment is shown above. Because the data are simulated, this estimate will vary slightly from run to run, but it should be reasonably close to the true value of 0.04.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers states that as the sample size increases, the sample mean converges to the true population mean.
In our case, this means that our estimator \(\hat\theta\) should get closer to the true value \(\theta = 0.04\) as we include more observations.

diff = A - B
running_mean = np.cumsum(diff) / np.arange(1, n + 1)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(running_mean)
plt.axhline(0.04, linestyle='--')
plt.xlabel("Number of observations")
plt.ylabel("Running estimate of θ")
plt.title("Law of Large Numbers in Action")
plt.show()








At the beginning, the estimate fluctuates substantially because the sample is still small. As more observations accumulate, the estimate stabilizes and moves closer to the true value of 0.04. This is exactly what the Law of Large Numbers predicts.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
Point estimates are useful, but they do not tell us how much uncertainty is attached to the estimate. To measure this uncertainty, we can use the bootstrap.
The bootstrap repeatedly resamples from the observed data and recalculates the statistic of interest. The spread of those bootstrap estimates gives us an estimate of the standard error.

boot_estimates = []

for _ in range(1000):
    A_star = np.random.choice(A, size=n, replace=True)
    B_star = np.random.choice(B, size=n, replace=True)
    boot_estimates.append(A_star.mean() - B_star.mean())

boot_se = np.std(boot_estimates)
boot_se

np.float64(0.017650398749036806)


For comparison, we can also compute the analytical standard error using the estimated Bernoulli variances.

piA_hat = A.mean()
piB_hat = B.mean()

se_analytical = np.sqrt(
    piA_hat * (1 - piA_hat) / n +
    piB_hat * (1 - piB_hat) / n
)

se_analytical

np.float64(0.017766823013696063)


The bootstrap standard error is very close to the analytical standard error, which gives us confidence that the bootstrap is working well in this setting.
Using the bootstrap standard error, we can construct a 95% confidence interval:
\[
\hat\theta \pm 1.96 \times SE
\]

lower = theta_hat - 1.96 * boot_se
upper = theta_hat + 1.96 * boot_se
(lower, upper)

(np.float64(0.003405218451887869), np.float64(0.07259478154811214))


This interval gives a range of plausible values for the true difference in conversion rates between the two CTAs.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
The Central Limit Theorem states that as the sample size grows, the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal.
To illustrate this, I repeatedly simulate the A/B test at several different sample sizes and plot the resulting sampling distributions of \(\hat\theta\).

def simulate_theta(sample_size):
    results = []
    for _ in range(1000):
        A_sim = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, sample_size)
        B_sim = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, sample_size)
        results.append(A_sim.mean() - B_sim.mean())
    return results

sizes = [25, 50, 100, 500]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 8))

for ax, s in zip(axes.flatten(), sizes):
    vals = simulate_theta(s)
    ax.hist(vals, bins=30)
    ax.set_title(f"n = {s}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Estimated difference")
    ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








When the sample size is small, the sampling distribution is rough and less symmetric. As the sample size increases, the distribution becomes smoother and more bell-shaped. This illustrates the Central Limit Theorem in practice.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing
We now test whether the two CTAs perform differently.
The hypotheses are:

\(H_0: \theta = 0\)
\(H_1: \theta \neq 0\)

We compute the test statistic
\[
z = \frac{\hat\theta}{SE}
\]
using the analytical standard error.

z = theta_hat / se_analytical
z

np.float64(2.1388179513414762)



p_value = 2 * (1 - norm.cdf(abs(z)))
p_value

np.float64(0.032450415036087366)


If the p-value is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the two CTAs differ in performance.
In this simulated example, the p-value is small enough to suggest evidence against the null hypothesis. That implies CTA A performs better than CTA B in this experiment.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression
A useful insight from statistics is that the difference-in-means test can also be written as a regression model:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i
\]
where:

\(Y_i\) is whether visitor \(i\) signed up,
\(D_i = 1\) if the visitor saw CTA A,
\(D_i = 0\) if the visitor saw CTA B.

In this setup, \(\beta_1\) captures the difference in average outcomes between the two groups.

Y = np.concatenate([A, B])
D = np.concatenate([np.ones(n), np.zeros(n)])

df = pd.DataFrame({"Y": Y, "D": D})

X = sm.add_constant(df["D"])
model = sm.OLS(df["Y"], X).fit()

model.params

const    0.178
D        0.038
dtype: float64



model.bse

const    0.012569
D        0.017776
dtype: float64



model.pvalues

const    1.865099e-43
D        3.265822e-02
dtype: float64


The regression coefficient on D is the same difference in means we calculated earlier. This shows that a simple A/B test can be analyzed as a regression problem, which is especially useful when researchers later want to add controls or extend the model.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
A common mistake in experimentation is peeking: repeatedly checking results during data collection and stopping the experiment as soon as significance appears.
This practice is dangerous because it increases the probability of false positives.
To show this, I simulate a setting where the null hypothesis is actually true:
\[
\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20
\]
Then I check significance every 100 observations and record whether the experiment ever produces a p-value below 0.05.

def one_experiment():
    A_null = np.random.binomial(1, 0.20, 1000)
    B_null = np.random.binomial(1, 0.20, 1000)

    for k in range(100, 1001, 100):
        A_k = A_null[:k]
        B_k = B_null[:k]

        theta_k = A_k.mean() - B_k.mean()
        se_k = np.sqrt(
            A_k.mean() * (1 - A_k.mean()) / k +
            B_k.mean() * (1 - B_k.mean()) / k
        )

        if se_k == 0:
            continue

        z_k = theta_k / se_k
        p_k = 2 * (1 - norm.cdf(abs(z_k)))

        if p_k < 0.05:
            return 1
    return 0

results = [one_experiment() for _ in range(1000)]
np.mean(results)

np.float64(0.205)


The proportion shown above is the false positive rate under repeated peeking. It is typically well above 5%, even though the null hypothesis is true. This demonstrates why experiments should have pre-specified stopping rules rather than being monitored continuously without adjustment.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Conclusion
This simulation-based A/B testing exercise illustrates several core ideas from classical frequentist statistics.
First, the Law of Large Numbers shows that our estimator becomes more stable as sample size increases. Second, the bootstrap provides a practical way to estimate uncertainty. Third, the Central Limit Theorem explains why normal-based inference becomes reasonable in large samples. Fourth, hypothesis testing gives us a formal method for evaluating whether observed differences are likely due to chance. Finally, the peeking example highlights why good experimental design matters just as much as the statistical test itself.
Overall, this example shows how simulation can make abstract statistical ideas much more concrete and intuitive.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text: Blueprinty is a small software company that makes tools for engineering firms that are preparing blueprint-based patent applications. The marketing team wants to make a strong claim: firms that use Blueprinty’s software are more successful at getting patents approved. Ideally, we would test this by observing the same firms before and after they started using Blueprinty, or by randomly assigning some firms to use the software and others not to use it. That ideal data does not exist here. Instead, Blueprinty collected data on 1,500 mature engineering firms, including each firm’s number of patents awarded over the last five years, regional location, age since incorporation, and whether the firm is currently a Blueprinty customer. This makes the question interesting, but also difficult. Blueprinty’s customers were not randomly selected, so a simple comparison between customers and non-customers could mix together the effect of the software with other differences between the firms, such as age or region. The goal of this post is to use Poisson regression and maximum likelihood estimation to make a more careful comparison.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
section: A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
text:
A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
The outcome variable is a count, so a Normal model is not a natural first choice. Patent counts cannot be negative, and they only take integer values such as 0, 1, 2, and 3. A Poisson distribution is a better starting point for this type of outcome because it is designed for non-negative count data.
For one observation, the Poisson probability mass function is:
\[
f(Y_i \mid \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}
\]
Assuming the observations are independent and identically distributed, the joint likelihood for all firms is:
\[
L(\lambda \mid Y_1, \ldots, Y_n) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}
\]
Taking logs turns the product into a sum:
\[
\ell(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[-\lambda + Y_i\log(\lambda) - \log(Y_i!)\right]
\]
The maximum likelihood estimate is the value of \(\lambda\) that makes the observed patent counts most likely.

Y = blueprinty["patents"].to_numpy()

def poisson_loglikelihood(lam, Y):
    """Log-likelihood for iid Poisson data with one common lambda."""
    if lam <= 0:
        return -np.inf
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * np.log(lam) - gammaln(Y + 1))


lambda_grid = np.linspace(0.1, 8, 300)
loglik_values = [poisson_loglikelihood(lam, Y) for lam in lambda_grid]

best_lambda_grid = lambda_grid[np.argmax(loglik_values)]
sample_mean = Y.mean()

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(lambda_grid, loglik_values, linewidth=2)
plt.axvline(sample_mean, linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label=f"Sample mean = {sample_mean:.3f}")
plt.axvline(best_lambda_grid, linestyle=":", linewidth=2, label=f"Grid maximum = {best_lambda_grid:.3f}")
plt.title("Log-likelihood for the simple Poisson model")
plt.xlabel("lambda")
plt.ylabel("Log-likelihood")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








The curve reaches its highest point close to the sample mean of patent counts. Visually, this means the best single Poisson rate for the whole dataset is the average number of patents per firm.
Mathematically, we can see the same result by taking the derivative of the log-likelihood:
\[
\ell(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[-\lambda + Y_i\log(\lambda) - \log(Y_i!)\right]
\]
\[
\frac{\partial \ell(\lambda)}{\partial \lambda}
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[-1 + \frac{Y_i}{\lambda}\right]
= -n + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_i}{\lambda}
\]
Setting this equal to zero gives:
\[
-n + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_i}{\lambda} = 0
\]
\[
\hat{\lambda}_{MLE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_i = \bar{Y}
\]
This result makes intuitive sense: in a simple Poisson model with only one rate parameter, the best estimate of that rate is the observed average count.

# Optimize over log(lambda), then transform back, so lambda is always positive.
simple_result = minimize(
    fun=lambda theta: -poisson_loglikelihood(np.exp(theta[0]), Y),
    x0=np.array([np.log(Y.mean())]),
    method="BFGS"
)

simple_mle = np.exp(simple_result.x[0])

simple_mle_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": ["Numerical MLE", "Sample mean"],
    "Value": [simple_mle, sample_mean]
})

display(
    simple_mle_table.style
    .format({"Value": "{:.6f}"})
    .set_caption("Simple Poisson MLE compared with the sample mean")
)

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Poisson Regression
The simple model assumes every firm has the same patent rate, which is too restrictive. A more useful model allows the expected patent count to vary by firm characteristics:
\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)
\]
\[
\lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta)
\]
The exponential function is important because \(X_i'\beta\) can be any real number, but \(\lambda_i\) must be positive. In this model, each firm’s expected patent count depends on its age, age squared, region, and Blueprinty customer status.
I include age squared because the effect of firm age is unlikely to be perfectly linear. I include region indicators because regional differences could affect patent output. One region must be dropped as the reference category to avoid perfect collinearity with the intercept. Here, Northeast is the reference region.

X = pd.DataFrame({
    "intercept": 1.0,
    "age": blueprinty["age"],
    "age_sq": blueprinty["age"] ** 2,
})

for region in sorted(blueprinty["region"].unique()):
    if region != "Northeast":
        X[f"region_{region}"] = (blueprinty["region"] == region).astype(int)

X["iscustomer"] = blueprinty["iscustomer"]

X_matrix = X.to_numpy(dtype=float)
Y = blueprinty["patents"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
terms = X.columns.tolist()

def poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X):
    """Poisson regression log-likelihood with lambda_i = exp(X_i beta)."""
    eta = X @ beta
    lam = np.exp(np.clip(eta, -50, 50))
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * eta - gammaln(Y + 1))


manual_result = minimize(
    fun=lambda beta: -poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X_matrix),
    x0=np.zeros(X_matrix.shape[1]),
    method="BFGS"
)

beta_hat = manual_result.x

# Compute a numerical Hessian of the log-likelihood at the MLE.
hessian = approx_hess(
    beta_hat,
    lambda beta: poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X_matrix)
)

vcov = -np.linalg.inv(hessian)
manual_se = np.sqrt(np.diag(vcov))

manual_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "term": terms,
    "coefficient": beta_hat,
    "std_error": manual_se,
    "incidence_rate_ratio": np.exp(beta_hat)
})

display(
    manual_results.style
    .format({
        "coefficient": "{:.4f}",
        "std_error": "{:.4f}",

Interpreting the coefficients
The customer coefficient is positive, which means Blueprinty customers have higher expected patent counts after controlling for age, age squared, and region. Its incidence rate ratio is about 1.23, so the model estimates that Blueprinty customers have about 23% higher expected patent counts than otherwise similar non-customers.
The age coefficient is positive and the age-squared coefficient is negative. This suggests that expected patent counts increase as firms get older, but the increase slows down for older firms. That pattern is sensible: young firms may patent less because they are still building capabilities, while mature firms may become more productive, but the advantage does not grow forever at the same rate.
The region coefficients are relatively small in this model. Since Northeast is the reference group, each regional coefficient compares that region to the Northeast, holding the other variables fixed. The main result of interest is that the Blueprinty customer coefficient remains positive even after adding these controls.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The Effect of Blueprinty’s Software
The Poisson regression coefficients are multiplicative, not additive. So the customer coefficient does not directly say “Blueprinty adds this many patents.” To express the result in patent-count units, I create two counterfactual datasets:

X0: every firm is treated as a non-customer.
X1: every firm is treated as a Blueprinty customer.

The two datasets keep each firm’s age and region unchanged. The only thing that changes is customer status.

X0 = X.copy()
X1 = X.copy()

X0["iscustomer"] = 0
X1["iscustomer"] = 1

yhat_0 = np.exp(X0.to_numpy(dtype=float) @ beta_hat)
yhat_1 = np.exp(X1.to_numpy(dtype=float) @ beta_hat)

average_effect = np.mean(yhat_1 - yhat_0)
avg_noncustomer_prediction = np.mean(yhat_0)
avg_customer_prediction = np.mean(yhat_1)

counterfactual_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Counterfactual scenario": [
        "All firms treated as non-customers",
        "All firms treated as Blueprinty customers",
        "Average difference"
    ],
    "Average predicted patents": [
        avg_noncustomer_prediction,
        avg_customer_prediction,
        average_effect
    ]
})

display(
    counterfactual_results.style
    .format({"Average predicted patents": "{:.3f}"})
    .set_caption("Estimated average effect of Blueprinty customer status")
)

The model estimates that if all firms were treated as non-customers, the average predicted patent count would be about 3.44 patents over five years. If all firms were treated as Blueprinty customers, the average predicted patent count would be about 4.23 patents. The difference is about 0.79 additional patents per firm over five years, holding age and region fixed at each firm’s observed values.
This result is consistent with Blueprinty’s marketing claim. In the data, Blueprinty customers have higher patent counts, and that positive relationship remains after controlling for age, age squared, and region. However, this is still an observational study. We cannot fully rule out unobserved differences between customers and non-customers. For example, firms that choose Blueprinty may already be more organized, better funded, or more serious about patenting. So the analysis provides evidence that Blueprinty customer status is associated with more patents, but it does not prove pure causality in the same way a randomized experiment would.
